strengths: The benchmark is genuinely well-motivated and addresses real gaps in competitive-programming evaluation: expert-designed test suites (vs. LLM/rule-generated tests), subtask-level partial scoring, direct human-contestant comparisons, and an offline judge that avoids dependence on online platforms.

The dataset construction is documented in detail (72 contests across 14 Olympiads, 403 problems, ~60 test cases/problem), with sensible quality-assurance steps: executing official solutions as ground truth to validate the judge, discarding problems with invalid solutions, and handling batch/interactive/output-only problem types separately.

Benchmarking is extensive: 32 models with multiple complementary metrics (pass rate, relative score, human percentile, medals, Elo), and the finding that GPT-OSS-120B achieves a higher pass rate than Gemini-2.5-Pro but lower percentile/Elo nicely illustrates why pass rate alone is insufficient.

The analyses go beyond a leaderboard: per-algorithm-tag breakdowns, subtask-position effects, temporal analysis against knowledge cutoffs (no evidence of contamination), parallel vs. sequential inference scaling, error-type distributions, and a reasoning-behavior taxonomy applied to traces.
The 'no temporal degradation around knowledge cutoffs' analysis (Fig. A3) is a useful contamination check that many benchmark papers omit.
weaknesses: The availability artifacts are not verifiable at review time: the 'Website:' field on the title page is literally blank, and all data, code, and leaderboard results are only promised for the future. Several headline claims (official/public test cases, reproducible offline evaluation) therefore cannot be checked by reviewers or readers yet.

The claim of 'expert-designed private tests sourced directly from official competition organizers' is overstated: Section 3 and Appendix A.1 admit substantial supplementation from CSES, LibreOJ, GitHub, and LLM-inferred metadata (Gemini-2.0-Flash fills missing tags/difficulty). Table 1's checkmarks ('official and public', 'Expert Test Cases') gloss over these caveats, and the Easy/Medium/Hard difficulty buckets inherit the noise of LLM-inferred difficulty scores.

The central human-comparison protocol favors models: models generate 8 candidates and submit the solution with the highest judged score, i.e., they receive per-problem oracle test feedback that human contestants never had within a contest. This asymmetry weakens the headline conclusion that GPT-5 (81.76th percentile) 'falls short of top human contestants'; a single-shot comparison should also be reported, and no variance/significance analysis over contests is provided.

Elo and contestant matching rely on name/country matching via Google Search to Codeforces profiles, with no reported accuracy of the matching; several contests in Table A6 have only 5-7 matched contestants, and USACO (132 tasks, the largest single source) has no human results at all, so percentile claims rest on a partially matched, contest-biased subset (46 of 72 contests).

The reasoning-trace analysis (Section 5.2) uses GPT-OSS-120B as the annotator of behavior segments, with no human validation of annotation precision reported; conclusions like 'stronger models allocate tokens more strategically' are correlational, and the suggested causal takeaways are speculative.

Ethical treatment is not addressed: automatically linking named (mostly minor) Olympiad contestants to Codeforces profiles and publishing ratings/percentiles raises privacy concerns that the paper does not discuss, nor is there a limitations section.

Novelty is incremental given concurrent work (OI-Bench, AetherCode, HLCE, LiveCodeBench-Pro, CodeELO); the comparative Table 1 is self-graded and a few entries (e.g., USACO marked non-'Updates' despite monthly releases) invite scrutiny.
